A former professional athlete on selling real estate to other athletes

💡 Key Takeaways
  • While it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it.
  • Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.
  • when he was hired to work for Tony Parker, his former teammate, in San Antonio, Texas; he started as a financial advisor for professional athletes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it. “You come as a problem solver, not a fan,” he noted.

Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.

Sangaré came to the U.S. when he was hired to work for Tony Parker, his former teammate, in San Antonio, Texas; he started as a financial advisor for professional athletes. During COVID, he moved into real estate, specializing in finding homes for athletes instead.

Recent findings suggest that sangaré explains that the pros tend to make a lot of money for a short period of time, and for that reason they’re usually interested in buying investment properties (often right after they’ve found homes for themselves and their family members). A massive part of their real estate agents’ job, then, is to keep their eyes on investment properties with the potential for strong returns.

Recent findings suggest that athletes have specific needs. “As a rookie, they’re just starting out, and they may not want to buy,” Sangaré told Taylor Anderson at eXpcon in Salt Lake City last month. Depending on the length of the contract, a rental might be a better idea. “There are times you tell people now’s not the right time to buy. If they feel you’re working in their best interests, they will trust you,” remarked Sangaré, who is part of eXp’s relatively latest sports and entertainment division (which several brokerages offer).

You have to be patient when working with athletes, he mentioned, since their situations are tied to ever-changing contracts; of course, players can be traded, and have to move promptly. You also have to be prepared to wait and work with them as they grow in their careers.

What you don’t have to be: A major follower of their particular sports. Sangaré admits that as a European, he doesn’t know much about football or baseball, but that doesn’t stop him from working with athletes in those sports. Sometimes not being starstruck helps him work with a more level head, he mentioned.

Sources indicate that but you do need to know the nuances of sports contracts. For example, some leagues, like the NBA, offer several-year guarantees, while others, like the NFL, don’t; housing options will vary based on those.

It has been revealed that often the connection to an athlete client comes through their financial advisor or sports agent, Sangaré mentioned. “The sports agent is always talking to the player, and he’ll know to reach out to you when someone gets traded,” he said.

But that can be a long road. Sangaré said it can take anywhere from five months to two years from starting a relationship with a sports agent to seeing any traction with a player, but you want to start that relationship early since once their clients do start to get traded, they’ll undoubtedly be approached by many other real estate agents. One practical tip he gives is going to the NBA Summer League in Las Vegas and taking agents out for coffee or lunch. “You have to be present where they’re present,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that and when you do get connected to the client, make sure you don’t start with a sales pitch. “You can’t try to sell them something right away,” Sangaré remarked; instead, you want to counsel them on how they can protect themselves and what they really need to know when buying a home — whether as an investment property or to live in.

Hoskinson: Cardano Not Done Yet

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to Cardano founder Charles Hoskinson, there is plenty more to come for Cardano, as the blockchain's privacy-preserving sister chain, Midnight, reaches a huge milestone as its ecosystem continues to expand.
  • Charles Hoskinson made sure to clear up misunderstandings about whether he thought the work on Cardano was done.
  • In a recent development, "I never once mentioned Cardano is finished," Hoskinson said in a Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to Cardano founder Charles Hoskinson, there is plenty more to come for Cardano, as the blockchain's privacy-preserving sister chain, Midnight, reaches a huge milestone as its ecosystem continues to expand.

Charles Hoskinson made sure to clear up misunderstandings about whether he thought the work on Cardano was done.

In a recent development, "I never once mentioned Cardano is finished," Hoskinson said in a Nov. 15 post on X.

The comments came after he talked about the completion of Cardano's original roadmap, which raised some questions about his role in the blockchain's future.

He also called out the CEO of the Cardano Foundation, Frederik Gregaard, for not mentioning the Midnight chain when discussing everything the network has accomplished.

In his latest video, uploaded on Nov. 17, Hoskinson celebrated the fact that Midnight had just brought on board its first UK-based banking partner, Monument Bank.

Monument Bank is the first UK bank to offer interest-bearing tokenized retail deposits on a public blockchain, according to an announcement from the Midnight Foundation.

Up to £250 million in customer deposits will be added to Midnight in the first phase, and each tokenized deposit will be backed 1:1 by sterling cash held at the bank.

Monument Bank customers can now earn a fixed 5.2% annual equivalent rate on deposits for 12 months, all without having to deal with cryptocurrencies directly.

Hoskinson was very excited about the scale of the initiative, comparing the planned amount of deposits with the current decentralized finance ecosystem on Cardano.

"It's five times the TVL of Cardano," he remarked.

The £250 million is the planned initial size of the banking product, not a verified figure for how much is currently deposited on Midnight.

Hoskinson called this one of the most key milestones in his career.

"This is just one of the many things to come, but I think it's one of the most significant things of at least my career," he remarked.

He added that the team behind Midnight had moved the originally scheduled hard fork from December to November to accommodate the technical needs of Monument Bank.

Despite the milestone, Hoskinson emphasized that it's only the first step in a much larger mission: bringing traditional financial assets onto Midnight.

It has been revealed that "This mission is not done if these assets are just strictly staying on Midnight. Needs to be expanded to Web3. But inherit from Midnight in terms of safety, security, privacy, simplicity," he stated.

According to recent reports, hoskinson thinks the main barrier to cryptocurrency adoption is the lack of trust among consumers. He believes that simplifying the user experience without compromising regulatory requirements will allow billions of people to join the blockchain economy.

Hoskinson also shared that there's a massive event coming up for the Midnight Foundation on Dec. 15. Developers will showcase future products and technological advancements scheduled for 2027.

  • The Fed also released its meeting calendar for 2027.
  • Finally, NAR reported existing home sales at an annualized rate of 3.75 million in October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last Week’s Highlights: No shortage of substantial news last week, but for mortgage rates, what mattered the most was bad inflation data coupled with a Fed that turned sharply hawkish again. Last week’s inflation data came in higher than expected and the most worrisome part was that the drivers were broad-based. It looks like core PCE, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, is set to come in around 0.3% month-over-month this year, or 3.2% year-over-year, which would mean that it’s moving in the wrong direction relative to the Fed’s target.

The Fed also released its meeting calendar for 2027. It will hold the usual 8 meetings, but the October 2027 meeting will be a strategy meeting where they will not change rates. As a result, they’re moving the December 2027 meeting to November. Even though this means 9 weeks instead of the usual 6 between policy meetings at the end of 2027, this should have minimal effect on monetary policy.

Finally, NAR reported existing home sales at an annualized rate of 3.75 million in October. That’s the lowest rate since August 2010 and lower than any month these last four years. This is consistent with Redfin data showing a historically low level of housing demand.

Upcoming Attractions: The biggest piece of economic data this week is the Tuesday retail sales report, which will give another look at how consumers are faring, but is unlikely to move rates much.

Industry observers note that investors will also get a chance to dissect the minutes from the last Fed meeting on Wednesday. And we will hear from other key FOMC members throughout the week. The ones to watch are Latest York Fed President Williams today, tomorrow, and Wednesday; Fed Chair Warsh today; Cleveland Fed President Hammack today, tomorrow, and Thursday; and Fed Governor Waller tomorrow.

Chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. Previously, she was an executive director leading housing finance and financial markets research at the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Prior to joining JPMCI, Chen was an economics consultant at Analysis Group, Inc., where she worked on financial litigation cases and led teams conducting health economics and outcomes research on behalf of pharmaceutical companies. While in graduate school, Chen was with the Center for Economic Studies and the Social Economic and Housing Statistics Division at the US Census Bureau, where she conducted applied microeconomics research using large scale restricted-access linked survey-administrative data. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics.

The XRP price is struggling to take advantage of institutional credibility for the ledger. Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse has another explanation: Wall Street is pulling liquidity toward blockbuster IPOs.

Industry observers note that the XRP Ledger Foundation assessed the network against all ten principles in the Global Layer One (GL1) Market Infrastructure Toolkit. CertiK independently verified the network’s evidence under the Architecture and Resiliency principles.

Garlinghouse said investors have been moving money out of crypto, including XRP, to fund major listings. He expects the market to recover after Anthropic’s debut, just as it did following SpaceX’s IPO.

According to recent reports, the GL1 toolkit gives financial institutions a common framework for assessing digital infrastructure. It has ten principles that cover governance, legal foundations, settlement finality, architecture, economic models, resilience, access, interoperability, privacy, and operations.

This makes the assessment relevant to banks exploring tokenized markets. Institutions need to understand how networks handle operational risk, governance, and settlement before building financial products on them.

The XRP Ledger Foundation has completed the attestation of the XRP Ledger against the Global Layer One (GL1) Market Infrastructure Toolkit. It is the first public, permissionless layer-1 blockchain to have the toolkit's Architecture and Resiliency principles independently… pic.twitter.com/wEKczeEdrF.

XRPL’s case is notable because it is public and permissionless. Traditional financial networks often operate behind controlled access. Public blockchains must show how risks are handled across distributed governance, protocol upgrades, and open participation.

The Foundation assessed XRPL against all ten principles. It also supplied supporting evidence for each control. CertiK then examined the Architecture and Resiliency sections, using code, configurations, logs, and test results.

CertiK noted it reviewed all 112 controls in the toolkit. Its technical verification focused on those suitable for independent assessment. The firm also verified Partior’s self-attestation under the same two principles.

Institutional adoption of digital assets depends on trust backed by independent verification and evidence.CertiK has completed independent technical verification of @XRPLF’s and Partior’s self-attestations under the Global Layer One (GL1) Market Infrastructure Toolkit,… pic.twitter.com/nQoEXjDHLh.

It has been revealed that the XRPL Foundation called it the first such verification for a public, permissionless Layer 1. The milestone gives institutions a structured reference when evaluating networks for tokenized deposits, stablecoins, funds, and other assets.

That is useful progress for XRPL’s institutional pitch. Risk and compliance teams can now examine evidence against familiar market-infrastructure standards. They have more than a blockchain’s own description of its capabilities.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • BrightAI Inc., a startup that helps industrial companies detect malfunctioning equipment, has raised $97 million in funding.
  • Smith Point Capital led the Series A round.
  • Many industrial machinery malfunctions affect internal components that aren’t visible to an outside observer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:37 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

BrightAI Inc., a startup that helps industrial companies detect malfunctioning equipment, has raised $97 million in funding.

Smith Point Capital led the Series A round. BrightAI stated in its Wednesday announcement of the deal that a number of other venture capital firms contributed as well. They were joined by GE Vernova Inc., an energy equipment firm that emerged from the 2024 split-up of General Electric Co.

Many industrial machinery malfunctions affect internal components that aren’t visible to an outside observer. As a result, complications often go unnoticed until they cause a major disruption. Palo Alto, California-based BrightAI develops hardware and software tools that help customers spot issues earlier.

The first component of the manufacturer’s product portfolio is a collection of sensors called State Stickers. They’re small, rectangular devices with a ruggedized case and a long battery life. Technicians can attach them to industrial equipment to monitor for complications that can’t be detected visually.

Industry observers note that the motion of a machine’s internal components produces noise and  vibrations that tend to follow a specific pattern. If an industrial fan’s blades rotate 30 times per minute, it might give off a whooshing sound every two seconds. BrightAI’s State Stickers can detect when a machine diverges from its usual operating pattern.

The sensors wirelessly transmit their measurements to a device called the Stateful AI Hub. It runs artificial intelligence models that analyze the data for signs of hardware failures. According to the tech giant, its models become more accurate as the number of sensors deployed at a site grows.

It has been revealed that brightAI offers software that enables companies to augment the data from its sensors with drone footage. A utility, for  example, could use a BrightAI-powered drone to detect erosion at the top of an electric pole. The tech giant’s AI models automatically draw a square around damaged components to spare technicians the hassle of manually analyzing footage.

Recent findings suggest that the firm indicates that its software can also collect maintenance data in other ways. A BrightAI-powered drone can read the meters that are attached to assets such as data center coolant tanks to check their internal pressure. Furthermore, built-in support for infrared cameras enables the software to spot overheating equipment.

The third core component of BrightAI’s product portfolio is an AI wearable. The Stateful Wearable, as it’s called, provides technicians with troubleshooting advice in the field. It also checks whether they follow safety guidelines during inspections and automatically turns maintenance data into reports.

Industry observers note that “Our infrastructure is under more strain than it has ever been, and Physical AI has finally become reliable enough to work in the field,” stated founder and Chief Executive Alex Hawkinson. “Bringing those two facts together is a once-in-a-generation opportunity.”.

BrightAI indicates that its products monitor hundreds of thousands of industrial assets across 50,000 sites. Investor GE Vernova, which is also a customer, looks to expand its use of the organization’s technology in connection with this week’s funding round. BrightAI, for its part, will use the capital to grow its international presence.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The home where Woodrow Wilson lives as a professor before becoming president has hit the market in Princeton, NJ for $5.85 million.
  • The Tudor Revival at 82 Library Place was built in 1896 for Wilson and he lived there with his wife, Ellen, and their three children until 1902, when he became president of Princeton University and moved on campus.
  • The home was first listed in May 2025 for $6.5 million.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The home where Woodrow Wilson lives as a professor before becoming president has hit the market in Princeton, NJ for $5.85 million.

The Tudor Revival at 82 Library Place was built in 1896 for Wilson and he lived there with his wife, Ellen, and their three children until 1902, when he became president of Princeton University and moved on campus.

The home was first listed in May 2025 for $6.5 million.

“Wilson and his wife had a lot of input in the design and finishes chosen for the home, which included double stained-glass doors from the Sears catalog,” indicates listing agent Barbara Blackwell of Callaway Henderson Sotheby’s International Realty.

The estate is one of only two working homes in the U.S. designed and built by a president, the other being Monticello, according to the listing.

Blackwell indicates the house has had 19 owners since the Wilsons, including Princeton University itself, which used the home as faculty housing during the Great Depression.

The current owners spent seven years restoring the property with architect Ron Berlin and Baxter Construction. The award-winning project brought back the original beams and woodwork and re-glassed the leaded windows. It also gave the home a distinct sense of presidential charm, making it easy to imagine Wilson tucked among its interiors.

The work also restored the stucco and timber exterior, added a cedar shake roof and a generator, and updated all mechanical systems.

The three-story home includes seven bedrooms and 5.5 bathrooms. Wilson once taught students in the spacious foyer, which opens to a wood-paneled library the current owners added. Stained-glass pocket doors lead to a dining room with a commissioned mural of campus landmarks.

The kitchen pairs restored original cabinetry with newly introduced matching pieces. It also has a copper drainboard sink, a working dumbwaiter, and a double Wolf range. Nearby, a new glass-roofed sunroom with a wet bar overlooks the grounds.

“The sunroom is a perfect blends interior and exterior with views of the gardens and flowering trees,” Blackwell states.

Of the four bedrooms on the second floor, one is a soundproofed primary suite with a coffee bar and a radiant-heated marble bathroom that opens onto a balcony. The skylit third floor contains three more bedrooms, a bathroom, laundry and a cedar walk-in closet.

Outside, the recently redesigned gardens surround two patios, a fountain and a koi pond. The 0.74-acre lot also has a circular driveway lined with boxwoods, an office in a former porte cochere and a restored, oversized two-car garage in the same Tudor style as the house.

The property is in Princeton’s Western Section and backs up to the current home of the university’s president. Nassau Street’s shops and restaurants are a short walk away.

“This home represents a substantial piece of history with all the modern conveniences of a fresh home,” Blackwell indicates. The owner’s collection of Wilson books and memorabilia can be bought separately.

#133438. Latest Update: Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (813 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (813 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that want to price more precisely?
  • When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds.
  • But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers stated no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

Expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

A sold comp tells us where a buyer noted yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

Sources indicate that imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

Suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:.

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

Sources indicate that that’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

It also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”.

In a recent development, when I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

Maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

Recent findings suggest that this is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

Listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

So, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:.

“I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”.

Sources indicate that twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

Sources indicate that find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

Sources indicate that sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:.

We’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:48 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

A bipartisan group of more than two dozen congressional lawmakers mentioned today they’re forming a newly introduced AI Safety and Innovation Caucus to tackle the growing security risks posed by the advances in sophisticated artificial intelligence models.

It has been revealed that the lawmakers cited the July hack of Hugging Face Inc.’s servers by a team of autonomous AI agents developed by OpenAI Group PBC, which broke out of an isolated sandbox environment, as an example of these risks. They also pointed to another incident involving the now-public Anthropic PBC, which also reported that its agents escaped their testing environments to access third-party systems.

These incidents have “underscored the need for Congress to better understand these risks and develop policy solutions,” mentioned Representative George Whitesides (D-California), a co-chair of the caucus. “As AI capabilities accelerate, so do the potential consequences of catastrophic misuse, loss of control over advanced systems and threats to national security.”.

Industry observers note that whitesides (pictured) is co-chairing the caucus alongside Representatives Nathanial Moran (R-TX) and Don Beyer (D-Virginia). In a post on X, they stressed the need for bipartisan collaboration to create the basic policy guardrails for AI safety, citing the growing concerns of the American public.

Industry observers note that does it feel like there's a new tech or AI crisis every day? Recent headlines are raising serious concerns about our digital safety and security.

Today, I'm joining @RepDonBeyer, @RepNateMoran, and over 20 of our colleagues to launch the bipartisan AI Safety and Innovation… pic.twitter.com/bhMyygy1J6.

In a recent development, — Rep. George Whitesides (@Rep_Whitesides) November 19, 2026.

The 26-member caucus includes seven Republicans, which is a surprising number given that the White House administration under President Donald Trump has strongly opposed any heavy-handed regulation of the AI industry. The goal of the caucus is to identify “targeted solutions” that ensure AI remains under control without derailing innovation and threatening America’s lead in the industry.

Whitesides mentioned the lawmakers will focus on two things: proposing legislation to augment AI safety, and responding quickly to high-profile security incidents by gathering developers, independent experts and government officials to brief lawmakers and come up with solutions.

“We want to be a conduit through which effective, responsible legislation can be refined and brought to the floor of the House,” Whitesides told Politico in an interview. He said the group will work together to propose, provide feedback and endorse new AI legislation. He believes there’s an urgent need for this, because most other groups within the House are more focused on educating members or creating legislation within their own parties, he said.

Another thing the caucus intends to do is to pursue relationships with outside AI experts who can help lawmakers to navigate complex policy decisions. It also wants to help raise public awareness around AI and its safety issues, and ensure members outside of relevant committees have the tools they need to contribute to new legislation and debate.

In the recent midterm elections, Americans made it clear that AI is becoming a major issue for governance. Moreover, a recent survey revealed that 43% of Americans don’t trust either of the two major political parties to properly get a grip on AI safety, according to a one-pager that accompanied the press release.

According to recent reports, “Artificial intelligence affects every American, and it should not be a partisan issue,” Moran noted. “This caucus gives us a place to find the areas of consensus, set partisanship aside and put smart, targeted policies in place so we can innovate while we keep people safe. Congress needs to be prepared.”.

There's a good chance this quick recovery turns into something more significant sooner than we anticipate. XRP is trading at $0.9927, up around 11% from the $0.89 low of the drop. XRP hadn't been below $1 since mid-August, when it dropped under that level for the first time since November 2024. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.
  • Industry observers note that the “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing.
  • In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

Industry observers note that the “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

“Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont said in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”.

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

“The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon remarked in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”.

According to recent reports, seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

The terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

Recent findings suggest that “Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan mentioned in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an important step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”.

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

In a recent development, inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

The solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

Industry observers note that “I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel said. “I think it’s important to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”.

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker said workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

Tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

According to recent reports, “A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really important component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker remarked. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”.

Bitcoin mining giant MARA Holdings, formerly known as Marathon Digital, continues to offload its Bitcoin holdings, with another multimillion-dollar transfer spotted as the manufacturer's selling spree highlights no signs of slowing down.

According to blockchain analytics platform Lookonchain, MARA transferred another 366 BTC, worth approximately $23.33 million, from its wallets on Nov. 18.

The latest transaction follows a series of substantial Bitcoin sales by the mining company throughout 2026.

Lookonchain estimates that MARA has already sold a staggering 40,581 BTC this year, generating approximately $3.03 billion at an average selling price of $74,446 per coin.

However, it remains unclear whether the latest 366 BTC transfer represents another completed sale or an internal movement of funds.

MARA's aggressive selling strategy is confirmed by its latest quarterly financial disclosures.

In a recent development, according to its Nov. 9 SEC filing, the firm sold approximately 26,984 BTC for $1.9 billion during the first nine months of 2026.

Following the end of September, MARA liquidated another 13,597 BTC at an average price of approximately $81,039, raising an additional $1.1 billion.

These transactions bring its total disclosed Bitcoin sales to 40,581 BTC.

Notably, the company used $750 million from its latest sales to fully repay Bitcoin-backed loans, releasing 17,477 BTC previously pledged as collateral.

Interestingly, MARA has explicitly signaled that it intends to continue selling Bitcoin as part of a broader shift in its corporate strategy.

However, it began allowing sales of newly mined Bitcoin in 2025 before expanding the policy in 2026 to include coins already held on its balance sheet.

In its latest shareholder letter, MARA said it prepares to continue monetizing Bitcoin to strengthen its financial flexibility.

The company specifically identified artificial intelligence infrastructure, upcoming convertible debt obligations and potential share repurchases as reasons for building up cash reserves.

The selling comes as MARA faces considerable pressure on its core mining business.

Third-quarter revenue declined 35% year over year to $164.2 million, compared to $252.4 million in the corresponding period of 2025.

UPDATED 07:16 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

Data center backlash is pushing builders to show communities what they get in return, and public-private partnerships are becoming one answer. As the race for sovereign AI heats up, the question is shifting from where intellectual property lives to where compute runs and who profits from it.

Industry observers note that canada offers a sharp test case. A modern data hall employs few people, but its profits can fund the startups and jobs a region needs, according to Sharif Virani (pictured), chief executive officer of SPUR Innovation Center.

“There’s a substantial misnomer right now in the world that’s kind of landing from previous tech, where people think where your IP is where the wealth creation is going to be,” he remarked. “It’s not the case anymore. You have to make sure your inference happens in your country or in your region.”.

Sources indicate that virani spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and host Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed sovereign AI, reinvesting data center profits in local entrepreneurs and winning over residents through public-private partnerships. (* Disclosure below.).

It has been revealed that SPUR treats its Waterloo, Ontario, site as an innovation campus with an attached data hall rather than a pure data center. The tech giant reinvests about 10 percent of the campus’s data center profits in local entrepreneurs through a venture studio and takes first right of refusal on their office space and compute, Virani explained. Canada’s Dominion List counts more than 500 founders who have left for San Francisco, he noted.

“We have entrepreneurship at an all-time low, productivity at an all-time low [and] GDP in freefall,” he said. “That’s really the result. We’ve got to reverse that.”.

Sources indicate that one of SPUR’s early investments went to two international students who had full scholarships to the University of Toronto and internships lined up in San Francisco. Instead, they launched a startup called Auditorium AI and hired staff, according to Virani. The model also reaches Main Street, where on-campus hackathons helped a former long-haul trucker build AI software for logistics.

“AI allows these people who know the problem, who have earned the right to solve the problem, to mobilize technology to do it and make the lives of their friends, families and neighbors better,” Virani noted.

Their return, therefore, restores previously committed ADA to the treasury, making it available for future ecosystem initiatives and community-approved funding proposals.

This development comes days after the rejection of a proposal seeking 22 million ADA to purchase and tokenize copper, showing the governance community’s ability to vet project funding.

In a recent development, ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin has stated that crypto needs some of the features that made housing a safe investment for earlier generations. "We need the equivalent of those good properties that housing investment has, for modern digital assets," Buterin wrote in a post on X on Nov. 18.

Recent findings suggest that the post came a day after economist Peter Tulip published his own post on housing in Raleigh, North Carolina. According to Tulip, looser zoning rules in the city set off a construction boom and pushed real rents down 15% between 2022 and 2025.

In his post, Buterin first pointed to a benefit of young people putting their savings into stocks and crypto instead of real estate.

"One benefit of younger generations investing more in stonks and other digital things instead of housing is that it reduces perverse incentives that drive people to push to keep housing expensive, instead of rejoicing when prices drop as we do for all other life necessities," he wrote.

According to recent reports, still, the Ethereum co-founder stated that housing has had one advantage over stocks and crypto. He described it as "a culture and policy-encouraged default of investing in a safe non-crazy thing that you can't easily liquidate.".

"Modern platforms encourage the opposite of this, leading to more irresponsible behavior," Buterin added.

Ether was trading at $1,808 on Wednesday.

Buterin has written about housing and urban planning before. He has supported the YIMBY movement for denser development in cities for several years.

In 2022, Buterin argued for a land value tax. According to him, such a tax would lower the upfront cost of buying a home and discourage speculation on vacant lots.

In 2025, the Ethereum co-founder called the housing market a "confusing market of peculiar NFTs." According to Buterin, what is really being sold under the label of square footage is the right to live in a particular city. At the time, he also noted that legalizing dense development speeds up the economy and benefits even people who prefer single-family homes.

Industry observers note that privacy coins are poised to be among the biggest cryptocurrency stories of 2027, driven by growing concerns over financial surveillance, institutional adoption, and the future of digital privacy. This creates a compelling investment narrative. Google Gemini AI predicts that two projects, Monero (XMR) and Zcash (ZEC), will stand out, and it aims to forecast which will experience a significant price surge in 2027.

According to recent reports, both Monero and Zcash are established leaders in the privacy-focused cryptocurrency space, but they employ fundamentally different approaches to protecting consumers’ financial information. Monero offers privacy by default, while Zcash seeks to balance financial confidentiality with greater accessibility for institutional investors.

As a potential major crypto bull market approaches in 2027, investors may find two distinct opportunities for substantial returns. However, determining which option could deliver the biggest gains may yield surprising results.

Recent findings suggest that monero has long been considered the gold standard for transaction privacy. Unlike conventional cryptocurrencies, where transactions can be publicly inspected on a blockchain, XMR makes privacy an inherent feature of its network.

Sources indicate that it achieves this through ring signatures, Ring Confidential Transactions (RingCT), and stealth addresses, which conceal the sender, transaction amount, and recipient. Importantly, privacy is mandatory, not optional.

This gives Monero a compelling proposition as a digital cash alternative, especially as blockchain analytics grow more sophisticated and financial surveillance expands.

However, that same characteristic creates a significant obstacle: regulatory scrutiny. Exchanges in several jurisdictions have restricted or removed XMR trading, potentially limiting access to a broader pool of investors.

Zcash takes a different approach, using zero-knowledge cryptography to enable shielded transactions while retaining the option of transparent transactions.

Its shielded addresses let owners conceal transaction details, while viewing keys let them selectively disclose information to auditors or other authorized parties. This flexibility could prove particularly attractive to institutions that want privacy without completely sacrificing compliance.

The distinction could become increasingly important as institutional investors look beyond Bitcoin and Ethereum for opportunities in specialized crypto sectors.

Industry observers note that privacy coins are already attracting attention beyond their traditional communities. Zcash has made considerable progress in positioning itself as a more institutionally accessible privacy network, with regulated investment products emerging and interest in its underlying technology growing.

Meanwhile, Monero continues to benefit from its established reputation, consistent privacy guarantees and decentralized architecture.

The broader investment narrative is also changing. As cryptocurrency adoption increases, more transactions become visible to blockchain analytics companies, incentivizing individuals and businesses to seek greater financial confidentiality.

However, the regulatory landscape could become a major obstacle in 2027. The EU’s Anti-Money Laundering Regulation is scheduled to apply from July 10, 2027, with restrictions covering crypto-asset accounts involving anonymity-enhancing coins.

According to recent reports, crucially, the legislation’s definition encompasses privacy features that operate either systematically or optionally. This means neither project can assume its architecture provides an exemption.

Looking beyond daily price fluctuations, the weekly and monthly charts will be particularly important in determining which cryptocurrency has the strongest potential heading into 2027.

In a recent development, for Monero, the key technical consideration is whether it can establish a sustained higher-high structure following its previous major market cycle. A successful retest of former resistance zones as support could lay the groundwork for another substantial move, particularly if capital rotates toward privacy-focused assets.

XMR also benefits from a relatively predictable supply model. Its permanent tail emission produces 0.6 XMR every two minutes, with an inflation rate that gradually declines over time.

Sources indicate that zcash, meanwhile, has a more conventional fixed supply of 21 million coins, giving it a familiar scarcity narrative. Its longer-term technical outlook will depend heavily on whether it can maintain gains tied to its growing institutional profile and establish stronger historical support.

Both could benefit enormously from a broader cryptocurrency bull market, although ZEC’s previous outperformance means investors should also consider the possibility of profit-taking and deeper corrections.

Users have two things to take care of before the service ends.

First, the remaining card balance has to be withdrawn: the Withdraw button on the Global Card page sends the funds to the Fiat account.

Sources indicate that second, subscriptions linked to the card should be cancelled or switched to another payment method. Unfortunately for cardholders, recurring payments will most likely fail if they stay on the old card.

It has been revealed that if there's still a balance when the service ends, MEXC will credit it to the Spot account, so customers will simply receive their funds back. It's crucial to keep in mind that pending card transactions need time to settle, which is why the balance snapshot comes on November 21, three days after the shutdown. The amount will be credited within three business days of the snapshot. Users do not need to take any action.

Refunds for previous card transactions will be credited to the Fiat account once MEXC receives them. Pending cashback will be credited automatically as scheduled. Elite VVIP users with zero-fee benefits will be refunded too, though the eligible fees return to their Spot accounts only before December 15.

Transaction history, card orders and cashback records stay available on the Global Card page for three months after the service ends, so it's worth saving anything needed before access ends.

Cryptocurrency services delegate certain types of services to third parties all the time, so witnessing a similar situation is more than a possibility here. Realistically, the shutdown is somewhat inconvenient rather than dangerous, as the balances are returned automatically. For users: stay vigilant and try not to put all your eggs in one basket.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Enterprises racing to build AI factories and push edge inference into the field are learning that buying graphics processing units is the easy part.
  • According to recent reports, those physical limits shaped much of the high-performance computing and AI conversation at SC26, where commercial AI infrastructure increasingly shares the floor with scientific computing.
  • “When we look at the full stack, we recognize that customers are getting tripped up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 07:55 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

Enterprises racing to build AI factories and push edge inference into the field are learning that buying graphics processing units is the easy part. Power, cooling and network throughput now decide whether those costly systems produce intelligence or sit idle.

According to recent reports, those physical limits shaped much of the high-performance computing and AI conversation at SC26, where commercial AI infrastructure increasingly shares the floor with scientific computing. Rack densities that once topped out at about 10 kilowatts are now on a path toward a megawatt, a step change that forces enterprises to look both above and below the traditional network, storage and compute layers, according to Jack Hogan (pictured), senior vice president of advanced growth technologies at SHI International Corp.

“When we look at the full stack, we recognize that customers are getting tripped up. They can go get the GPUs, but they can’t power them. They can’t cool them,” Hogan said. “These are not cheap systems either. Procuring the infrastructure is just the start.”.

It has been revealed that hogan spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed edge inference and how power, networking, model choice and business outcomes are reshaping the way enterprises build and run AI infrastructure. (* Disclosure below.).

It has been revealed that the economics of AI infrastructure are shifting along with the hardware. Enterprises once sized deployments by the rack unit or the rack, but entire data centers now operate as a single system with shared memory, and every GPU must be kept fed to justify its cost. That change has altered how SHI measures success, Hogan explained.

“Now we’re talking about row and now data center scale. … We’re measuring that now in megawatts,” Hogan noted. “So the megawatt now starts to become a measurement that people start to grasp and understand. How many flops can you get through that megawatt? How fast can you process your tokens?”.

SHI’s role spans the full life cycle of these systems. Drawing on 37 years in the industry, the manufacturer builds customized racks in its integration facilities around the globe and runs pre-site assessments so systems can be powered on as soon as they arrive. In a recent Newly introduced Jersey project, SHI is hosting and operating the customer’s system in its own data center. Location matters at the edge, too, where workloads such as video input generate data that must be processed in place, Hogan noted.

“You can’t backhaul that. The networks are not necessarily the right way to move that,” Hogan said. “We’re creating the scenario of both the mega hyperscaler as well as the edge inference and be able to tie those two things together.”.

According to recent reports, busy GPUs are not necessarily productive ones. SHI starts every engagement by asking customers what they are trying to achieve, then works backward to the right model, whether that means frontier intelligence or a small language model running on an edge device. Silicon follows the same logic, with GPUs, newer CPUs, inference-specific chips and neural processing units validated in the organization’s AI and Cyber Lab.

Sources indicate that “It’s not about the cost of the token or reducing the number of tokens or even finding cheaper tokens. It’s about optimizing and ensuring that those tokens are turning into business value,” Hogan said.

  • In a recent development, the financing includes a $41 million Series B round led by Jump Capital with participation from Catalyst Investors, and a $23 million Series A round led by CRV and Susa Ventures.
  • Pulley has partnered with multifamily developers like Wood Partners, as well as large retailers, restaurants, banks, and manufacturers, including Amazon, Starbucks, JLL and Meta.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pulley, a development technology organization that helps multifamily and commercial development projects navigate permitting and approvals, has raised $64 million in new funding to expand its AI-driven services, the company unveiled this week.

In a recent development, the financing includes a $41 million Series B round led by Jump Capital with participation from Catalyst Investors, and a $23 million Series A round led by CRV and Susa Ventures. Pulley said the capital follows 5x year-over-year growth in annual recurring revenue and will support both expansion of its permitting business and new products aimed at compressing pre-construction timelines.

Pulley has partnered with multifamily developers like Wood Partners, as well as large retailers, restaurants, banks, and manufacturers, including Amazon, Starbucks, JLL and Meta.

Pulley operates in entitlement, due diligence and approvals, a part of the development lifecycle that has grown increasingly complex for multifamily and commercial real estate. The company estimates that 80% of project time is now spent before construction begins, as developers navigate zoning, environmental review, design iterations and building codes that vary widely across jurisdictions.

According to recent reports, “The speed at which we build is one of the most crucial challenges facing America over the next decade,” said Charlie Jacobson, Pulley co-founder and CEO, in the announcement. “To remain a global leader in AI, bring manufacturing back home, reach energy independence and sustain job growth, we need to build orders of magnitude faster. The single biggest lever to building faster is to get started faster.”.

Pulley remarked it combines AI-powered tools with a nationwide team of more than 75 licensed experts and a proprietary regulatory database to help clients secure approvals “faster and more predictably.” The company reports that it has supported $21 billion in commercial construction projects across all 50 states and thousands of cities and counties, saving customers a combined 11,750 weeks of project time.

It has been revealed that pulley’s services include diligence, approval strategies, construction plan reviews and coordination with local agencies. The company also participates in private plan review programs, allowing it to approve building looks directly in place of local jurisdictions in more than 2,000 cities and counties, according to the announcement.

Recent findings suggest that the company said customers typically see just one round of comments from permitting authorities per project, and more than 40% of projects are approved without any feedback. Pulley reported that projects on its system have received 65% fewer review comments this year compared with 2025, as its models and rules engine learn from each submission.

According to recent reports, with the new funding, Pulley plans to extend beyond permitting into other pre-construction decisions that affect cost and schedule. New capabilities will combine zoning and permitting data with utility availability, local sentiment and other constraints to help owners and developers evaluate sites and programs.

Pulley is also rolling out AI-assisted drawing review designed to flag building code compliance complications earlier in design, reducing redesign cycles and surprises during blueprint check.

Lengthy permitting and entitlement timelines are a major driver of project risk and carrying costs for residential and commercial developers, particularly in high-growth markets where local agencies are understaffed and regulations are changing quickly. For build-to-rent sponsors, single-family developers and multifamily owners, a slow or unpredictable approvals process can derail capital plans and delay unit delivery into tight markets.

Recent findings suggest that tools that standardize and partially automate permitting, codify jurisdictional rules and centralize reviewer feedback are increasingly seen as a way to protect returns and reduce soft costs. Pulley’s growth and new capital signal continued investor interest in technology focused on the “paper side” of development rather than just construction itself, and could accelerate adoption of private proposal review and AI-enabled compliance checks across more jurisdictions.

Cardano-based stablecoin DJED has revealed its sunset, as DJED and SHEN services will wind down on December 31, 2026, at 11:59 pm UTC.

DJED represents a crypto-backed, overcollateralized stablecoin protocol on Cardano whose US-dollar peg is maintained algorithmically against an ADA reserve (with SHEN as the reserve coin), rather than by fiat reserves.

"DJED and SHEN services will wind down at the end of December 31, 2026, at 11:59 pm UTC," a DJED-focused X account wrote.

Sources indicate that ATTN: DJED & SHEN Holders DJED and SHEN services will wind down at the end of December 31, 2026 at 11:59pm UTC. Please redeem and convert any DJED and SHEN you hold before then. All redemptions are subject to the reserve ratio.

People are urged to redeem and convert any DJED and SHEN they hold before this deadline. Users are to redeem on the protocol and convert their DJED and SHEN back to ADA on the official Djed page. Users who hold DJED or SHEN in liquidity pools, lending markets, or other DeFi platforms are urged to withdraw those positions first, then redeem or swap.

Sources indicate that the Djed team mentioned all systems are fully operational and redemptions are now open, subject to the reserve ratio. It further added that the Djed protocol will be maintained and remain available until December 31, 2026. After this date, all remaining funds will be allocated to the outstanding DJED/SHEN holders once the wind-down is complete.

According to recent reports, djed’s shutdown comes almost three years after its launch, which came in 2023. The stablecoin was officially rolled out on the Cardano mainnet on January 31, 2023, and was developed by COTI in collaboration with the Cardano ecosystem to be used on DeFi protocols on Cardano as a stable alternative to volatile cryptocurrencies.

In positive news for the Cardano ecosystem, Monument Bank Limited has introduced tokenized deposits on the Midnight network, marking a milestone for the network and the decentralized finance ecosystem.

At present, Monument is the first UK bank to tokenize retail deposits on a public blockchain, offering clients a 5.2% AER fixed-term return on savings directly through its existing banking app, delivering institutional onchain finance through a familiar and user-friendly banking experience.

Up to £250 million of client deposits will be represented on Midnight in this opening phase, with deposits recorded one-to-one in sterling.

West Capital Lending hit with 1099 independent contractor suit

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1078 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A former branch manager has filed a proposed class-action lawsuit against West Capital Lending (WCL), renewing questions about how mortgage companies use independent contractors and 1099 compensation structures for their staff in California.
  • 12 in the Superior Court of California for the County of Orange, Jason Heaps alleges that Irvine-based WCL misclassified him and other California workers as independent contractors, depriving them of wages, breaks and other protections owed to employees under state labor law.
  • WCL and Heaps did not respond to HousingWire’s requests for comment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A former branch manager has filed a proposed class-action lawsuit against West Capital Lending (WCL), renewing questions about how mortgage companies use independent contractors and 1099 compensation structures for their staff in California.

In a complaint filed Nov. 12 in the Superior Court of California for the County of Orange, Jason Heaps alleges that Irvine-based WCL misclassified him and other California workers as independent contractors, depriving them of wages, breaks and other protections owed to employees under state labor law.

WCL and Heaps did not respond to HousingWire’s requests for comment.

According to the complaint, Heaps began working for WCL in November 2023 as a branch manager. In January 2024, he also took on internal technology responsibilities, including customer relationship management (CRM) administration, software development and systems integration. His employment ended in September 2025.

Heaps claims WCL classified him as a 1099 independent contractor while paying him a fixed recurring amount regardless of hours worked and still exercising control over his work. He alleges he reported to a manager, worked from an assigned office in Irvine, did not submit invoices, regularly worked more than 40 hours per week without overtime pay and did not receive his final paycheck after his employment ended.

Industry observers note that “This treatment was not merely occasional, but reflected Defendants’ pattern and practice of willfully misclassifying Defendants’ employees as independent contractors,” the lawsuit states.In a statement to HousingWire, Morgan & Morgan founder John Morgan and attorney Michael Sigall, who represent the plaintiff, remarked they had filed “a class action lawsuit against West Capital Lending, Inc. alleging the company misclassified workers as independent contractors when they should have been treated as employees.”“As a result, workers were allegedly denied basic wage and hour protections California law guarantees. Hardworking people deserve to be paid every dollar they’ve earned, and we are committed to holding West Capital accountable,” they wrote.

WCL, which has about 1,900 sponsored LOs and originated about $10.8 billion year-to-date, has been the target of several lawsuits over its business and employment practices in recent years. Competitors, including loanDepot and Griffin Funding, along with former employees, have filed actions challenging the manufacturer’s model. WCL has denied wrongdoing in those cases.

Recent findings suggest that the 1099 independent contractor structure is also part of loanDepot’s ongoing lawsuit against WCL. In that case, loanDepot alleged that WCL misclassified about 600 loan officers as independent contractors, paying them on a 1099 basis and avoiding employment-related costs.

“loanDepot’s investigation has revealed that all of its former California loan originators poached by WCL who still hold California licenses to originate loans switched from operating under the standard MLO license issued by the Department of Financial Protection and Innovation (DFPI), which requires mortgage loan originators to be employees of their sponsoring lender, to a ‘real estate salesperson with MLO endorsement’ license issued by the DRE [Department of Real Estate] after joining WCL,” the loanDepot complaint states.

The loanDepot complaint alleges that WCL’s California LOs perform exclusively mortgage loan origination duties, not real estate sales activities. WCL allegedly classifies its California originators as independent contractors while treating those in other states as employees. (WCL also sued loanDepot, alleging Truth in Lending Act violations).

Industry observers note that california Labor Code Section 2775 codifies the so-called ABC test for determining whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor. However, Section 2778(c)(1) excludes qualifying real estate licensees from the ABC test and directs their classification to California Business and Professions Code Section 10032(b).

That provision allows real estate brokers and salespersons to establish their relationship as either employer-employee or independent contractor. For other purposes under the Labor Code, the Borello multifactor test, which is a more flexible, fact-specific analysis, generally applies.Under the ABC test, which applies to most workers, an individual is presumed to be an employee unless the hiring entity establishes all three conditions: The worker is free from the manufacturer’s control and direction, both under the contract and in practice; performs work outside the usual course of the company’s business; and is customarily engaged in an independently established trade, occupation or business of the same nature as the work performed.

In the Heaps case, the complaint asserts that WCL’s treatment of the plaintiff “cannot meet any part of the ABC Test and Defendants knew it.”.

The DFPI referred questions about this licensing and employment model to the DRE, which did not respond to requests for comment. The Department of Industrial Relations, which enforces labor law, also did not respond to questions.

The use of 1099 models for loan originators and branch personnel has become a flashpoint in California, where some lenders argue that compliance-focused firms are at a competitive disadvantage.

Alan Pezeshkian, president of California-based House America Financial, remarked he is not opposed to 1099 compensation structures in principle but is concerned about inconsistent application of labor and tax standards.

“When companies gain a competitive advantage by circumventing employment and tax laws, it creates an uneven playing field and penalizes those of us who make compliance a priority,” Pezeshkian said. “Let’s call it what it is: when a tech giant improperly classifies employees as independent contractors to avoid payroll taxes and other employment obligations, that’s not innovation, that’s just gaming the system. And when that becomes a recruiting strategy, companies that follow the rules are effectively being punished for doing the right thing.”.

Troy Garris, co-managing partner at Garris Horn LLP, remarked the inquiry under many laws focuses on control versus independence.

“Under many laws, a worker is an employee if the business can dictate not just what is done, but how, when and where it is done, and by whom. Independent contractors, by contrast, run their own businesses: they set their own methods, use their own tools, take on the risk of profit or loss, and are free to work for other companies,” Garris said. “Some laws make proving contractor status especially difficult, such as under California’s ABC test.”.

Colgate Selden, a founding member of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and a shareholder at Baker Donelson, said hiring 1099 independent contractors, from a regulatory perspective, is a “dangerous game” because the definition of “employee” touches multiple regimes.

It has been revealed that “Regulation Z does not define employees,” Selden said. “If a term is not defined within the regulation, you look to the contract and state law. So, then that’s gray.”Update: This story has been updated to include a statement from the plaintiff’s attorneys.

Considering the history of the transferred funds, the move has sparked speculation that the hacker might already be preparing to spend the stolen funds, further sabotaging Binance’s chances of full recovery.

However, it is key to note that there is no evidence that the attacker has sold the Ethereum, as the receiving wallet has not been identified.
