Sources indicate that jeff Bezos says Nvidia should look inside the tech giant for its next CEO, and he doesn’t give an outsider much chance of success. The Amazon founder, now co-CEO of AI engineering startup Prometheus, made the comments Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event.

“If you don’t bring Jensen back, I would not hire an outsider. Nvidia is too complicated,” Bezos mentioned. Outside CEOs at complex companies, he added, “have a vanishingly small chance of succeeding,” and he would consider hiring one “a last resort.”.

Sources indicate that nvidia’s board claims it has no prepares to bring Huang back. Harvey Jones, the longtime director named the manufacturer’s first board chair last week, opened Nvidia’s earnings call Tuesday afternoon by saying the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”.

Jones said the search will include internal and external candidates, and that the board wants a permanent CEO in place quickly but won’t rush the pick.

Huang, the Nvidia co-founder and CEO for 33 years, had posted a statement on X that morning offering to return. He said he had “made serious mistakes” in his personal life and would cooperate with the board’s independent investigation.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the organization, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote.

It has been revealed that nvidia declared Huang’s resignation last Thursday, a day after the Upcoming York Times reported that he’d had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Days earlier, he admitted to an affair with a woman who U.S. officials believe was recruited by Chinese intelligence, according to the Wall Street Journal.

CFO Colette Kress, who spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career, is serving as interim CEO.

Two major Nvidia investors, Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, asked the board to leave open “the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives wrote in a note Sunday that talk of a Huang comeback is “ridiculous.”.

The Amazon precedent (not really): Bezos has been through a founder handoff of his own. He turned over the Amazon CEO job in 2021 to Andy Jassy, a longtime insider who built AWS. When Semafor raised the comparison, Bezos called it a poor one, saying there has never been a more carefully planned transition.

In a recent development, he stated he didn’t know enough about what happened in Nvidia’s board meetings to say whether Huang should return. But he called Huang a remarkable founder who deserves “admiration and respect no matter what.”.

In a recent development, huang himself remarked in a Bloomberg interview recorded Oct. 14 that he hoped his successor was already inside the company.

The Nvidia comments came in a wide-ranging interview. Bezos also said Blue Origin is using Prometheus tools on two projects, called President Trump by far the most communicative of the presidents he has worked with, and said Robert Pattinson was the clear choice to play the next James Bond after screen tests of five finalists.

Business as usual, officially: Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier, including $107.6 billion from its data center business. On the call, it raised its forecast for next fiscal year’s revenue growth to about 75%, from 70%.

Industry observers note that kress didn’t mention Huang by name on the call. Asked about the leadership transition, she remarked customers, suppliers and employees remain behind the company, calling it “business as usual.” She ended the call with a short pep talk that finished, “We’ve got this.”.

In case the board was wondering about one outsider in particular, Bezos is spoken for. During the Semafor interview, he described running Prometheus as “Nirvana.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:15 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 11:49 am.

Washington’s biggest economic threat may be the conviction that it’s already doing everything right.

That was the pointed warning from a Technology Alliance panel Tuesday, where a conversation about talent and economic growth became a challenge to the state’s self-image as an innovation leader.

“You noted spicy, right?” Rob Ogburn asked, taking up the invitation to speak bluntly.

“The economy is very strong. The economy is not competitive at all,” said Ogburn, executive director of Business and Community Services at Central Washington University.

While tech giants such as Microsoft and Amazon and sectors including aerospace and biotech are powering today’s economy, that doesn’t mean Washington is positioned to win tomorrow’s investment, develop its workforce or spread opportunity beyond its major employment centers.

Amelia Ransom, former vice president at Smartsheet and past Nordstrom leader, questioned the definition of success, arguing that future growth also depends on investing in people and businesses outside the corporate spotlight.

Recent findings suggest that “Who do we mean when we say winning? Who is it? Who are we talking about, and who are we leaving out?” Ransom said, later adding, “We have to close the daylight between who we say we are and who we actually are.”.

The panel was held in downtown Seattle and moderated by Jolenta Coleman-Bush, director of Microsoft Philanthropies. It also included Rachel Smith, president of Washington Roundtable.

Rather than simply calling for more talent and innovation, panelists examined how Washington develops the people already here, whose perspectives inform its decisions and how effectively its institutions and stakeholders work together.

Recent findings suggest that unification is essential. U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., led the passage of the CHIPS and Science Act in 2022 to bolster semiconductor manufacturing and innovation in AI and energy. But her home state has received just 0.3% of the funding awarded so far, Ogburn stated.

He argued that other states and regions were more effective at uniting to make their case for investment, showing their collective resources and the problems they could solve.

“We showed up and noted, ‘We’re competing with our neighbor, and we’re better than them.’ No investor is going to look at that and say you’re going to make the best use of my money,” Ogburn said.

Cultivate talent, don’t just recruit it. Ransom compared workforce development to a restaurant, a grocery store and a garden: recruiting ready-made workers, developing the talent already here and growing the long-term pipeline.

Recent findings suggest that “The middle is where we probably need to spend more time, which is at the grocery store, which means you’ve got to learn to cook,” she said. Her point: Invest in Washington’s existing employees, students, and businesses.

Smith wants employers to identify the high-wage, high-skill jobs they need filled so educators and businesses can coordinate strategies to prepare workers for those roles.

According to recent reports, fill essential information gaps. Panelists called for a clearer picture of community skills and barriers to opportunity, more voices to challenge prevailing assumptions, and closer examination of how regulations affect businesses.

“We’ve gotten in this war of the rankings where everybody’s like, “No, we’re the best. No, we’re the worst.” And we we’ve got to stop doing that,” Smith said.

The region needs data-backed insights into the reasons behind the rankings, she said. Smith pointed to the recently formed Economic Development Council and its planned statewide strategy as a step toward a more coordinated approach.

Whether these efforts succeed, Ogburn stated, should be judged by the communities themselves.

According to recent reports, “And then, if you want to measure success, go back to those communities and ask them if they feel successful,” he remarked. “Do they have agency and self-determination?”.

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:36 pmNovember 17, 2026 at 6:36 pm.

Jeff Bezos has a space company, a newspaper, an AI startup that’s raised $14.5 billion and, apparently, a seat in the room when Amazon decides who gets a license to kill.

Speaking Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, the Amazon founder mentioned he was “heavily involved” in the casting of Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond, a pick Amazon MGM Studios revealed Monday.

Amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond franchise when it acquired MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, then took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

Bezos mentioned a large initial pool of would-be Bonds was narrowed to five finalists, who then did “real old-fashioned screen tests”: three scenes apiece, in full costume on real sets with other actors.

The other finalists were Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner, according to The Upcoming York Times, which reported that the tests took place in London in late October.

Bezos noted the decision-makers got together Friday and spent a couple of hours reviewing the screen tests before settling on Pattinson.

“By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing,” Bezos stated. “But there was something special about Rob Pattinson and his performances.” He said the group, including director Denis Villeneuve, reached a quick consensus. It was “kind of immediately undebated.”.

Bezos admitted that the group was initially “slightly biased” against Pattinson because he’s already so famous.

“We sort of thought, you know, maybe we should have somebody a little more unknown,” he said. “But in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond.”.

Since the prolonged price correction has continued to weaken investor confidence, it appears that the whales have acted upon the growing fear and withdrawn the assets they had initially committed to the Solana network to hedge against further losses.

Running from November 2026 to January 2027, the campaign will focus on digital and social media initiatives, destination content in Arabic and English, and flight and hotel offers available through Wego. The initiative aims to introduce travellers to different ways of experiencing Thailand, while making it easier to explore travel options that suit their interests and preferences.

In a recent development, at the heart of the campaign is TAT's "Healing is the New Luxury" positioning, which encourages travellers to look beyond conventional ideas of luxury and embrace experiences that support relaxation, connection and personal wellbeing. From discovering local traditions and regional cuisine to spending time in nature or enjoying a slower pace of travel, Thailand offers opportunities to make each holiday more personal.

Mamoun Hmidan, Chief Business Officer at Wego, mentioned: "Travellers from the GCC are increasingly looking for holidays that offer more than a change of scenery. Thailand is well positioned to meet these expectations, with its diverse hospitality offerings and rich cultural experiences. Through our collaboration with the Tourism Authority of Thailand, we are bringing these opportunities closer to GCC travellers, while making it easier for them to compare travel options and proposal a holiday that suits their needs.".

For GCC travellers, the country's appeal extends well beyond its established beach resorts and shopping destinations. Bangkok offers a blend of cultural heritage, contemporary dining and vibrant neighbourhoods, while Chiang Mai and Chiang Rai provide opportunities to experience northern Thailand's natural landscapes and local traditions. Along the southern coast, Phuket and Krabi offer settings for family holidays, private retreats and outdoor experiences.

In a recent development, ahman Mad-adam, Director of the Tourism Authority of Thailand (TAT) Dubai Office, remarked: "Thailand has always welcomed travellers from the GCC with warmth and hospitality, and we want to encourage them to discover the country from a fresh perspective. Beyond our renowned beaches and vibrant cities, Thailand offers a wealth of experiences rooted in local culture, nature and wellbeing. Our 'Healing is the New Luxury' campaign celebrates these experiences and invites visitors to enjoy Thailand at their own pace. Working with Wego allows us to bring this message to a wider audience across the Gulf and highlight the many possibilities Thailand offers for a memorable holiday.".

The campaign will also highlight Thailand's range of hospitality experiences, including wellness retreats, private pool villas, family-friendly resorts and halal-friendly dining options. By presenting a wider selection of experiences, Wego and TAT aim to help travellers consider destinations and activities that reflect their individual travel priorities.

The initiative also places greater emphasis on the experiences that shape a holiday, rather than simply the number of places visited. Travellers can explore Thailand through its food culture, traditional wellness practices, local communities and natural surroundings, with opportunities to combine relaxation and discovery within a single trip.

By combining TAT's destination expertise with Wego's regional reach and travel marketplace, the campaign will connect destination storytelling with practical planning tools, helping GCC travellers explore Thailand's diverse offerings and find flight and accommodation options for their next trip.

In a recent development, wego is the number one travel app and the largest online travel marketplace in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA). Combining a dynamic travel marketplace with on-platform bookings, Wego enables travelers to easily search, compare, and book flights and hotels across hundreds of airlines, hotels, and online travel agencies. Beyond its B2C marketplace, Wego also operates WegoPro, a next-generation business travel platform, and WegoBeds, a MENA-focused bedbank. The organization is dual-headquartered in Singapore and Dubai with offices in Bangalore and Mumbai.

ZetaChain's 55M ZETA Burn Isn't a One-Time Event: What Proposal 2 Really Does

💡 Key Takeaways
  • ZetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments.
  • Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn.
  • Sources indicate that zetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

ZetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments. Voting closes Nov 7.

Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn. Read the proposal's own schedule, though, and nothing close to 55 million disappears on the day the chain halts. The figure is real, but it arrives in twelve installments over 2027.

Sources indicate that zetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics. About 55 million ZETA of undistributed validator emissions will be burned monthly through 2027, following the schedule on which they would have been emitted. The roadmap in the same post puts the pace at twelve monthly burns of roughly 4.6 million ZETA each, from January to December 2027.

That detail changes how the number should be read. Most of the early flash coverage collapsed it into a single burn, which implies an immediate supply shock. The staged schedule tells a different story. These tokens were never going to circulate, because they are validator rewards for an L1 that is about to stop. Burning them on the original emission timetable keeps the published release schedule intact and introduces no upcoming mechanism, as ZetaChain's FAQ puts it.

Industry observers note that governance Proposal 2 builds on Proposal 68, which approved the move to Solana in September with 99.4% in favor. Proposal 2 supplies the mechanics. Voting runs 72 hours and closes on November 7, and ZetaChain notes nothing moves unless it passes.

Recent findings suggest that if it does pass, every ZETA balance is recorded at snapshot block 20,755,000, expected around December 9. The ZetaChain L1 halts at that same height and isn't restarted. Claims open the same day through the ZetaHub migration portal, and ZetaChain's newly introduced private AI app, ZetaLabs, debuts alongside it.

The proposal also pairs the migration with a upcoming whitepaper, which ZetaChain calls the document of record for the token after the move.

The snapshot goes well beyond a simple wallet count. It records liquid, staked, unbonding and unclaimed-reward balances. Staked ZETA is credited automatically, so nobody has to unstake, and exchange balances convert without any action from holders. Staking rewards stop at the snapshot height.

Holders who want to claim directly face a short process. They connect the wallet that held ZETA, sign a message naming a Solana wallet, and receive the full balance shortly afterward. The claim costs no fee and requires no SOL. According to the post, the portal asks only for a signature, never for a transaction or a seed phrase. A minimum of 10 ZETA at the snapshot is needed to claim.

Two edge cases deserve attention. First, ZETA wrapped or sitting in pools and contracts can't be claimed by a key, so holders need to unwrap and exit before the snapshot. Second, assets still held as ZRC-20 tokens at the snapshot can be claimed back on their original chain through a separate bridged-assets page, with a $5 minimum per token. Both are the kind of detail that catches people out when a deadline arrives.

On Solana, ZETA becomes a native SPL token under the same ticker, with 9 decimals and no freeze authority. The full snapshot total is minted before the portal opens, and then the mint authority is revoked, so no one can ever mint more. No third-party bridge is involved.

Industry observers note that that sequence is the strongest holder protection in the plan, and it is also the part that can be checked in public. The supply stays capped at 2.1 billion less whatever has been burned, and ZetaChain says it will publish the SPL mint address and the migration program address before December 9. Once those exist, anyone can compare the minted total against the snapshot and confirm that the authority was actually revoked. That confirmation deserves the most scrutiny.

In a recent development, meanwhile, the portal and its program are under independent review by Hacken, and ZetaChain claims the portal opens only after the review is complete and the report is published. The ERC-20 version of ZETA on Ethereum is unaffected by the proposal. Purchaser and core contributor vesting completes on January 1, 2027, and ZetaChain says no newly released ZETA will be sold in 2027.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest practical risk is inattention. Most holders don't need to do anything until December 9, but exchange users depend on each exchange's own conversion window, and anyone holding ZETA through a contract or pool has homework to do beforehand.

Sources indicate that scams add another layer of risk. Any migration with a claim portal invites imitators, and ZetaChain tells holders to trust only its official domains and social accounts. A simple rule of thumb helps here: a site that asks for a seed phrase should be closed immediately, since the legitimate flow only needs a message signature.

On the technical side, claims are checked against the published snapshot rather than the live chain, so they continue to work after the halt. ZetaChain states it will announce any change to the process in advance.

It has been revealed that the vote decides the terms, not the direction. If Proposal 2 fails, the direction approved in Proposal 68 stands and ZetaChain returns with a revised proposal. Nothing moves on these terms.

According to recent reports, if it passes, the sequence is clear. The security report, mint address and migration program address arrive before December 9. The snapshot, halt, mint and portal opening follow on the day, and the monthly burns run through 2027. ZetaLabs then adds a Premium tier in the first quarter of 2027, with ZETA as the token for access and payment.

Taken together, this looks more like a retirement proposal for an L1 than a dramatic supply event. The burn is gradual, the mint is capped, and the claim process is simple on paper. Execution is what will matter most: the audit report, the published addresses and the clean revocation of mint authority. Those are the items to watch between now and December 9.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:00 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 7:47 am.
  • Sources indicate that sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, unveiled a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion.
  • Panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:00 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 7:47 am.

Sources indicate that sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, unveiled a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion. To meet demand from Panasonic and other buyers, the manufacturer looks to expand its plant in Moses Lake, Wash., supporting roughly 500 additional manufacturing and construction jobs over the coming years.

Panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells. The silicon-carbon composite can replace some or all of the graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes to improve performance.

Sila began operations at its Moses Lake plant last year and has about 100 full-time employees at the site. The facility is still scaling up production, with initial capacity designed to supply batteries totaling about 2 gigawatt-hours — enough for roughly 20,000 to 50,000 EVs, depending on how the material is used.

The expansion will increase that capacity to tens of gigawatt-hours, stated Gene Berdichevsky, Sila’s co-founder and CEO.

“This is a really notable blueprint for reindustrializing the U.S.,” he said. “We have to take new technology and leapfrog China, not just copy what they’ve done over the last 20 years.”.

While the U.S. has expanded battery manufacturing, it still depends heavily on overseas suppliers for core materials and technologies, Berdichevsky remarked. Sila aims to strengthen that domestic supply chain with higher-performing components.

In a recent development, batteries support industries central to energy independence and national security. They power EVs, consumer devices, drones, robotics and hardware deployed in space, and provide backup electricity for data centers.

Industry observers note that berdichevsky said Titan Silicon can help a battery store 20%–40% more energy in the same space, cut recharging time roughly in half and deliver more power than a battery using a conventional graphite anode. The anode itself is also much lighter and smaller.

Recent findings suggest that in August, Sila received a conditional federal loan commitment of up to $1.4 billion through the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital to expand domestic battery technology manufacturing. The firm must meet financial, legal, technical and other requirements before the loan can be finalized.

Industry observers note that the startup previously received a $100 million grant during the Biden administration under a similar initiative to increase U.S. energy independence. Those funds helped build its plant in Washington.

It has been revealed that the company has also raised $1.6 billion from private investors, including a $300 million round announced in July. The 15-year-old company is valued at $2.27 billion, according to PitchBook.

According to recent reports, seattle-area startup Group14 also makes a silicon-carbon anode material. It operates a smaller-scale manufacturing facility at its Woodinville, Wash., headquarters and produces commercial-scale volumes at a plant in South Korea.

Group14 has partially completed its Moses Lake manufacturing site but repeatedly delayed the start of production. It now targets mid-2027 to bring the first of two production units online, with no firm completion date for the second. It recently declared intends for a factory in Spain.

Growth is key to bringing down costs and making Sila’s technology competitive in mass-market batteries, Berdichevsky said.

“This is really the beginning of chapter three for our firm’s history,” he stated.

Industry observers note that the first two chapters were inventing the technology and moving from grams to tons of production, he added. This phase is about reaching the mass market. Sila aims to begin manufacturing at the expanded facility in 2028, with output increasing over time.

Recent findings suggest that “None of this is easy,” Berdichevsky said. “It’s not the inventing technology; it’s the manufacturing of it that’s really really hard, and we’re going to try to more than 10x the scale from what we’ve already done.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Leading cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase has declared the official listing of artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic (ANT) shares on its trading platform in the U.S. and U.K.

Industry observers note that the listing comes as Anthropic, the company behind the popular AI chatbot Claude, officially made its much-anticipated stock market debut on Thursday, Nov. 19, with its shares seeing massive volatility.

Industry observers note that as per the latest X post from Coinbase, the exchange announced the availability of Anthropic (ANT) shares for eligible users in the U.S. and U.K.

Sources indicate that it's important to mention that ANT isn't a cryptocurrency but a traditional stock. Coinbase's support for ANT shares reveals the organization's efforts to expand its offerings beyond crypto into traditional financial markets.

Industry observers note that anthropic has set a newly introduced historic precedent, having successfully raised about $81 billion in its initial public offering (IPO). This is the biggest IPO ever.

The artificial intelligence company sold 980 million shares at $83 per share, significantly higher than its previously announced price range of $70 to $78.

This brought Anthropic's initial valuation to about $1.5 trillion, making the firm one of the most valuable publicly listed firms in the world right from the get-go.

But as Anthropic shares started trading on the Nasdaq exchange, the ANT ticker saw massive volatility.

As per Reuters, Anthropic shares began trading at $111.50. This represented an enormous 34% premium over the IPO price.

At the initial peak, Anthropic's market cap exceeded $2 trillion, surpassing SpaceX's valuation when it debuted on the market in June.

Recent findings suggest that anthropic shares slipped to around $95 as the stock gave back a significant chunk of its gains. This was partly due to investors looking to book their profits.

Nonetheless, Anthropic shares were still trading comfortably above their $83 IPO price.

The volatility surrounding Anthropic's stock market debut signals increasing doubts about the AI investment craze.

The listing of Anthropic shares is just one of Coinbase's moves to enter traditional financial markets.

Instead of just providing cryptocurrency trading, the exchange is looking to become a platform for multiple asset classes.

It has been revealed that interestingly, Coinbase had already listed Anthropic pre-IPO perpetual futures for eligible non-U.S. owners on Nov. 18.

The perpetual futures were derivative contracts that allowed traders to speculate on Anthropic's valuation before its shares officially started trading on Nasdaq.

In a recent development, with the latest listing, eligible Coinbase users in the U.S. and U.K. can now trade the publicly listed Anthropic shares.

Anthropic's blockbuster debut comes as financial markets have been rocked by recent volatility, with tech stocks and crypto facing selling pressure.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am.
  • Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle company talked about building for years but always found too big to take on.
  • The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting new software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am.

Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle company talked about building for years but always found too big to take on.

The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting new software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.

Recent findings suggest that “The ceiling on what we can accomplish is no longer limited by the speed at which we can build software,” stated Joe Duffy, the company’s co-founder and CEO, recounting the message he delivered to the Pulumi team. “It’s limited by how ambitious we’re willing to be and how massive we’re willing to dream.”.

Recent findings suggest that the ambition is all the more notable because Pulumi is getting smaller. The firm has about 100 employees, down from about 130 last year. Duffy said there were no layoffs, and that AI has changed people’s roles and made the company more efficient.

According to recent reports, annual recurring revenue per employee more than doubled over the past year, he remarked. The firm isn’t profitable yet, but it has had a few months of positive cash flow this year. Pulumi hasn’t raised money since 2023, when it landed a $41 million round led by Madrona, bringing its total to about $99 million over the company’s lifetime.

Pulumi’s co-founders include Duffy and Eric Rudder, both Microsoft veterans. They started the organization in 2017 to let engineers manage cloud infrastructure such as servers, networks and permissions by writing code in everyday languages like Python and TypeScript.

The new products take that approach further:.

In a recent development, to decide whether a change is safe to ship, Pulumi Delivery can use Jev, an AI model from TypeSafe AI that estimates the odds of specific risks the team asks about in a planned change. If a risk is higher than the threshold the team sets, the release stops.

Duffy said he first noticed TypeSafe in May when it signed up as a Pulumi customer, because he liked the name. A few months later, Jev took off and TypeSafe used Pulumi to expand worldwide.

“Now even the call on whether a change ships can be made by a model,” said Daniel Gafni, a member of the technical staff at TypeSafe AI, in the Pulumi announcement. “That’s exactly the kind of decision we built Jev to make.”.

Industry observers note that both products are available now in public preview. Some features, including Jev decision gates and setting up agents, require Pulumi’s paid Pro or Enterprise plans.

Lucky timing: Pulumi’s founding bet on everyday programming languages turned out to suit AI agents, which are trained to be very good at writing exactly that kind of code.

“I wish I could say I predicted that 10 years ago, but it turns out in this case, what’s good for humans is also good for agents,” Duffy said.

AI agents now handle 40% of the operations on the Pulumi platform that people used to do, up from 15% in April and none in January, Duffy said. Agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pulumi’s own Neo are making infrastructure changes on their own.

Duffy stated many companies building AI coding tools stop once the code is written and reviewed. “For them, life stops at the merge,” he said. The newly introduced products cover the steps after that, from testing through release.

Industry observers note that plenty of company: Pulumi won’t have this market to itself. Duffy pointed to Harness, which calls it the “agentic SDLC” (short for software development lifecycle), and GitHub, which pitched “agentic software delivery” at its Universe conference last month. He mentioned Cursor aspires to solve the problem and Anthropic built its own internal system.

The upcoming products could replace some of the work now done by tools such as Argo CD and GitHub Actions, along with lots of homegrown scripts, he remarked.

In a recent development, “This is an industry-changing moment, and somebody has to solve this problem,” Duffy mentioned. “And I think we are exceptionally well poised to do so.”.

Bring your own bot: Neo, the infrastructure agent Pulumi introduced last year, is now just one example of a Pulumi agent. Customers can set up as many as they want, each with its own job, instructions and tools. They can also bring their own agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, and run it in Pulumi’s cloud.

Neo itself, which ran mainly on Anthropic’s Claude, can now use models from OpenAI or Google, too. “It’s not just Anthropic anymore,” Duffy said.

Agents can start work from an alert in PagerDuty, Datadog or Honeycomb, on a schedule or on request, and they report back to teams in Slack.

Pulumi has briefed about 50 customers, and about a dozen are in a private beta. Duffy stated no launch in the manufacturer’s history has gotten a warmer reception, and he named Moderna among the customers eager to get it.

Pulumi has thousands of customers overall, including major companies such as BMW, Snowflake and Wiz.

Industry observers note that the business: Pulumi’s gross margins have stayed in the high 80s to low 90s even as agents drive up usage, Duffy mentioned. Many customers run Pulumi from inside their own Claude Code sessions, which means they’re paying both Anthropic and Pulumi.

In a recent development, duffy said Pulumi wasn’t out looking for money when it raised its last two rounds. Investors came to the tech giant, and each deal came together in about 48 hours.

Madrona’s Tim Porter has joined the board, Duffy remarked, taking the seat previously held by the late Soma Somasegar, who led Pulumi’s first investment.

Industry observers note that about 40 of the manufacturer’s 100 employees are in the Seattle area, working out of an office at Two Union Square. Duffy remarked Pulumi is hiring more people locally because in-person work still matters when building upcoming products.

Industry observers note that despite the smaller headcount, Pulumi is still hiring, including sales reps in nearly every region of the world. Inside the manufacturer, Duffy noted Pulumi is having a lot of success with “product-minded engineers who can think from our customers’ point of view, who can think like engineering managers, commanding a team of agents.”.

Asked whether a sale or more funding was in the cards, Duffy mentioned Pulumi aspires to be a long-term successful business. “There are a variety of ways to get there,” he said. “But we want to get there on our own terms.”.

webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and notes it tops Gemma 4 31B. The card's own footnotes show why the comparison deserves a re-run.

It has been revealed that A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500. The most revealing line in its model card isn't a score, though. It's a footnote saying the competitor numbers were never re-run.

webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers. The 8.8B-parameter reasoning model is post-trained from IBM's Granite 4.2 8B using full-parameter supervised fine-tuning, followed by GRPO/DAPO reinforcement learning. A final length-aware RL stage produces the "balanced" variant, which is the default.

It has been revealed that the card reports 98.2 on MATH-500 and 88.3 on AIME 2025. It says TwIL-8B posts the highest MATH-500 and LiveCodeBench scores in its comparison group, which includes Gemma 4 31B at about 3.5 times its size. That claim is worth testing, because small models that beat larger ones are exactly what open-weight owners want to hear.

It has been revealed that on MATH-500, the card lists TwIL-8B at 98.2, Qwen3.5-9B at 96.6 and Gemma 4 31B at 87.9. On AIME 2025, TwIL-8B scores 88.3 against 87.1 for Gemma 4 31B. On LiveCodeBench, TwIL-8B scores 81.6 against 80.0, though that figure carries a dagger marking it as measured on the verbose variant, not the default balanced one.

It has been revealed that the card is also more candid than most. It says TwIL-8B is not a knowledge model. GPQA Diamond comes in at 70.2, trailing Gemma 4 31B by 14.1 points, and the model also trails on MMLU-Pro and HLE. There is no safety or preference tuning beyond what Granite carries, and the license is non-commercial. That honesty makes the claims easier to weigh.

In a recent development, here is where the headline gets complicated. TwIL-8B's scores come from webAI's own internal high-effort pass@1 runs. The card states that competitor scores are published figures and were not re-run.

In a recent development, gemma 4 31B's 87.9 on MATH-500 comes from Red Hat's evaluation of an FP8 build, using the lighteval harness, not from Google. The card itself notes that this figure is unusually low and may reflect answer extraction. In other words, the 10.3-point gap that anchors the headline compares one team's own harness against a third party's number that the card suspects may be understated.

None of this makes TwIL-8B's result wrong. It means the margin isn't established until both models run under the same harness, prompt and sampling settings. For reference, Google's Gemma 4 model card is the source for several of the other Gemma figures in the table.

It has been revealed that read the whole table and the picture is more balanced than the headline suggests. In the card's head-to-head summary, TwIL-8B beats Gemma 4 31B on 3 of 14 shared benchmarks and loses 11. It leads on MATH-500, LiveCodeBench and AIME 2025, but trails on AIME 2026 (88.3 against 89.2), HMMT Feb 2026 (68.2 against 77.2), GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and IFEval.

It has been revealed that the AIME 2025 lead is the shakiest. The card says AIME and HMMT sets have 30 to 33 problems, so one problem is worth about 3 points, and gaps of that size sit within noise. A 1.2-point margin is well under one problem, so the result is best read as a tie.

Recent findings suggest that against the closest same-size rival, Qwen3.5-9B, the card indicates the models roughly level on contest math, with TwIL-8B using fewer tokens: about 19.5k per AIME 2026 problem against 31.2k. That efficiency claim may turn out to be the more durable one.

Sources indicate that the card makes replication unusually practical. The Q4_K_M balanced GGUF weighs 4.98 GiB and runs through llama.cpp, with a command given in the card. Larger Q8_0 and F16 builds exist only for the verbose variant. The model also needs a big generation budget, since a short limit truncates its reasoning and scores far worse. The card suggests settings around 32,768 new tokens and a 40,960-token context.

Anyone planning a check should expect three catches. First, the card notes all its scores were measured on bf16 weights, not the GGUF builds, so a CPU run tests a slightly different artifact, and the card expects small deviations, most likely at Q4_K_M. Second, MATH-500 is 500 problems and each answer can run to tens of thousands of tokens, so CPU testing will be slow. Third, the decoding setup matters, since the card says none of its numbers use low-effort or thinking-off modes.

For a fair comparison, the same prompt, answer extraction and sampling must be applied to Gemma 4 31B too, ideally at full precision.

In a recent development, the card also lists contamination caveats. Its training pools were decontaminated against AIME, HMMT Feb 2025 and 2026, MATH-500, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, HLE, IFEval, IFBench and LiveCodeBench using 13-gram matching. HMMT Nov 2025 and the HumanEval, MBPP and CRUXEval suites weren't in the decontamination set. The MATH-500 and AIME results fall inside the protected group, which counts in the model's favor.

Overall, TwIL-8B looks like a genuinely strong small model for contest math, code and instruction following, and the card is open about its weak spots. The claim to beat Gemma 4 31B is narrower than the headline suggests: a clear lead on one benchmark, a likely tie on another and a loss on most of the rest.

It has been revealed that the useful next step is a same-harness run of both models, with the bf16 weights as a control for the GGUF build. Until independent results appear, the 98.2 is best quoted as webAI's reported figure, and the size-beating framing is better described as unproven than wrong.

Vertex’s executive chairman: Here’s how we got our drug-trial success rate over 70% when the industry’s is 10% to 20%

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1158 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Corporate America is locked in an innovation arms race – a race that is turning out very few winners.
  • But more bets don’t necessarily produce more successes.
  • According to recent reports, there’s no more extreme example of this problem than pharmaceuticals and biotech.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Corporate America is locked in an innovation arms race – a race that is turning out very few winners. Companies are spending billions on R&D, acquisitions and new technologies, operating on the seemingly intuitive premise that making more bets is the best way to approach the uncertainty of the future.

But more bets don’t necessarily produce more successes.

According to recent reports, there’s no more extreme example of this problem than pharmaceuticals and biotech. It takes an average of 10 to 15 years for a drug to go from the lab to regulatory approval. And more than 90% of drugs that enter clinical development fail. Just look at the headlines: one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical companies recently suffered three drug trial failures in a single week despite an enormous R&D budget, many talented scientists and a deep pipeline.

But this problem is far from unique to healthcare. In consumer tech, many startups flame out after a single hit; in automotive, EV pioneers are routinely outpaced by fast followers; digital investments in retail often fail to translate into customer growth.

According to recent reports, the instinctive response when innovation fails is to do more of it: fund more projects, pursue more ideas, make more acquisitions and place more bets. If innovation is inherently unpredictable, the thinking goes, the best way to improve your chances of success is to increase the number of shots you take.

This kind of thinking is completely backward. It’s not about the shots. It’s about the target.

Imagine entering a darts tournament and throwing five consecutive bull’s-eyes, only to discover that you have been throwing at the wrong board. Your accuracy doesn’t matter. You’ve lost.

More activity creates the appearance of innovation without improving its effectiveness. I learned this the hard way.

It has been revealed that when I joined Vertex Pharmaceuticals in 2009, the company had spent two decades investing heavily in R&D across 20 different programs. Yet, it produced only a single breakthrough product, which was rendered obsolete just two and a half years later with the approval of a better and more tolerable treatment discovered by another company.

It has been revealed that when we examined why drug development failed so frequently, the problem wasn’t that scientists had failed to create a drug that hit its intended biological target. The problem was that they had chosen the wrong target in the first place.

The solution was to take away choices, constraining ourselves to a “sandbox” of diseases with genetically- or pharmacologically-validated targets where we believed we had a much higher probability of success.

Most importantly, both R&D and business development had to stay inside the same sandbox. A fascinating scientific discovery or enticing acquisition wasn’t enough. If it didn’t fit our strategy or if we didn’t have a validated target to address, we walked away.

In a recent development, that last part may be the most difficult lesson for any leader. Companies often celebrate the ability to say yes to innovation. Sustainable innovators also become very good at saying no. Focus and strategy don’t limit innovation, they accelerate it.

Industry observers note that A thriving innovation program requires many parts of an organization working in harmony. Yet companies unintentionally divide innovation into functional silos, with each group incentivized differently and no one focused on the substantial picture.

Researchers discover something and hand it to developers. Developers hand it to manufacturing. Eventually, commercial teams are asked to sell it. Business development may operate on a separate track entirely, hunting for external opportunities.

But a brilliant invention that cannot be efficiently developed, manufactured or commercialized isn’t a successful innovation.

It has been revealed that to break down internal silos, leaders from research, development, regulatory, manufacturing, commercial and other key business units should be included in decisions about fresh product development from the earliest stages of the innovation process. And internal and external innovation must be tightly integrated into the same strategy. Business development can’t be given permission to roam the universe looking for any interesting assets; partnerships and acquisitions must reinforce the same strategy, diseases, and targets where a company believes it has a high probability of success.

Recent findings suggest that innovation shouldn’t be measured by how many ideas an organization generates. It should be judged by how effectively the entire organization converts its best ideas into products that meet people’s needs and create meaningful value.

According to recent reports, once innovation succeeds, companies tend to become complacent and stop innovating to create better and better medicines for the same disease. Our experience seeing one of our breakthrough drugs quickly made obsolete by an innovative competitor created a sense of urgency, and even some paranoia, which drove our organization to continuously try to “out-innovate ourselves.”.

Being first doesn’t guarantee long term success. Competitors will learn from your breakthroughs and improve on the foundations you laid. We decided that if someone was going to build a better second-generation product, it should be us.

The results were dramatic. Vertex went on to develop multiple transformative medicines, including 5 medicines that alter the course of cystic fibrosis for 95% of patients and, with CRISPR Therapeutics, the first FDA-approved human gene-editing therapy for patients with severe Sickle Cell Disease and transfusion-dependent B-thalassemia. More recently we created a completely new class of non-opioid medicines for moderate to severe acute pain.

According to recent reports, even more important to me is what happened to the odds. Our R&D success rate, measured by positive Phase II proof of concept, exceeded 70% across six diseases — far above the 10% to 20% industry average. We didn’t eliminate risk. Innovation can’t exist without risk. But we became much more deliberate about which risks were worth taking and therefore more successful.

Before approving the next project, acquisition or moonshot, leadership teams should ask themselves an important set of questions: Do we understand why innovation has failed here before? Are we pursuing opportunities where we possess a genuine advantage? What evidence tells us that the underlying problem is solvable? Does this opportunity reinforce our existing capabilities – or merely distract from them? And, perhaps hardest of all, what are we willing to stop doing so that our best ideas have the resources to succeed?

According to recent reports, the innovation economy has conditioned leaders to admire the size of the pipeline, the number of experiments and the volume of bets. Those are measures of activity, not success.

The companies that sustainably innovate will not be the ones willing to make the most bets. They’ll be the ones that understand their odds better than anyone else and have the discipline to walk away when those odds aren’t good enough.

Bitcoin price has now lost more than 10% over seven days, with selling pressure spreading across equities, precious metals and other risk assets. Yesterday’s $582.3 million outflow from US spot Bitcoin ETFs added another blow, bringing November withdrawals close to $3.5 billion.

Recent findings suggest that blackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) accounted for $541.1 million of Thursday’s withdrawals, its largest single-day outflow since launching. The same session saw $727 million in crypto liquidations, with bullish traders absorbing most of the damage.

Institutional demand is weakening, leveraged buyers are being forced out, and the Federal Reserve’s increasingly hawkish outlook is making speculative assets less attractive.

Bitcoin is now approaching $60,000, a level that could determine if the correction finds a floor or develops into something uglier.

The ETF withdrawals are arguably the biggest concern for Bitcoin holders right now. Spot Bitcoin ETFs became an crucial source of institutional demand after launching in January 2024. Their buying helped absorb available supply and gave traditional investors a regulated route into the market.

Recent findings suggest that that demand is now moving in the opposite direction. US spot Bitcoin ETFs have lost more than $1.1 billion this week alone. November’s cumulative withdrawals have approached $3.5 billion.

The pressure extends beyond ETFs. Rising Treasury yields and expectations of another Federal Reserve rate increase in December have encouraged investors to reduce exposure to assets that offer no regular income.

In a recent development, meanwhile, derivatives traders are taking heavy losses. CoinGlass data indicated more than $700 million in liquidations across crypto markets over 24 hours. Long positions accounted for 86% of the total.

Bitcoin itself recorded nearly $202 million in liquidations, with bullish traders suffering the majority of forced closures.

This creates a difficult environment for buyers. Falling prices trigger liquidations, which create additional selling pressure and push prices lower. The reduction in open interest also suggests excessive leverage is being flushed from the market.

This is the bearish outcome. A decisive break below $60,000 could trigger another wave of stop-loss orders and leveraged liquidations.

The next downside area sits around $58,000, while more aggressive technical projections point toward $53,700.

This would give buyers time to absorb available supply without immediately reversing the entire November decline.

Scenario 3: Bitcoin reclaims $62K and debuts a relief rally.

A recovery above $62,000 would provide the first meaningful sign that sellers are losing control. A move toward $65,000 would then become possible, followed by resistance around $68,000.

Recent findings suggest that consistent ETF inflows, improving market sentiment, and a weaker dollar would strengthen this scenario. Without those developments, any rebound risks becoming another opportunity for sellers to exit.

For existing holders, the decision depends heavily on their entry price, investment horizon, and exposure. Long-term holders who bought substantially below current prices have more room to withstand volatility. Selling simply because Bitcoin crossed a psychological threshold risks locking in profits or losses without knowing whether the broader investment thesis has changed.

Recent findings suggest that however, investors holding leveraged positions face a different problem. Falling prices can trigger forced liquidations regardless of their long-term convictions. Reducing leverage and protecting available capital should take priority over waiting for a rebound.

For buyers, the temptation to buy the dip is understandable. Bitcoin is considerably cheaper than it was just weeks ago, but cheaper does not automatically mean undervalued.

Buying in stages rather than committing an entire allocation around $61,000 offers more flexibility if the market tests $58,000 or even $53,700.

Recent findings suggest that bitcoin price remains vulnerable to another leg down. The $60,000 level is no longer just a psychological milestone. It is where the next major battle between buyers and sellers will be fought.

#133309. Your Business Is Busy. But Is It Actually Growing? Ask These 4 Questions to Find Out.

Your Business Is Busy. But Is It Actually Growing? Ask These 4 Questions to Find Out.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1257 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten.
  • I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten. “You can get bigger, or you can get better,” he said, “but you can’t do both at once.”.

I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid. Work for my marketing agency, Bolt Marketing, slowed overnight, and I was on edge like everyone else. As the dust settled, it became clear that we had enough steady business to keep the lights on, so we made a call. We let go of our most exhausting clients and spent six months working on figuring out who we actually were as a company.

We tightened up our processes and got honest about our positioning — all the stuff we’d been ignoring. We’ve grown every year since, and I can trace almost all of that growth back to this period of intense focus.

I think about Jack’s line a lot this time of year, because the fourth quarter makes business owners a little crazy. The year is almost over, you’ve got revenue goals to hit, budgets to review, and everyone’s already asking about your intends for next year. For a lot of founders, the natural response is to put their heads down and work harder. I’ve done it plenty of times myself, and I’ve learned that a lot of that extra effort goes into motion that never turns into progress.

It has been revealed that I’ve spent most of my career working with entrepreneurs building businesses in smaller markets. They know exactly when payroll hits, and they’re building their companies without millions of dollars in outside investment. For them, time is as tight as cash. A business like that can stay incredibly busy for years while nothing really changes.

So before the year wraps up, it’s worth asking a few uncomfortable questions to make sure your time and effort are actually moving you forward.

Revenue is vital. I’m certainly not going to argue otherwise. But revenue alone can hide a lot. You can grow sales while your margins shrink. You can bring in fresh customers who are a nightmare to serve, or hire a bunch of people and add services only to discover you’ve built a more complicated version of the business you already had. I’ve watched founders post record sales and still end the year with less cash and less freedom than they started with.

Before you set another ambitious revenue target, look at what your growth is actually producing. Are you more profitable? Is your team getting stronger? Are your customers happier? Is the business becoming less dependent on you? Those questions will tell you a lot more about whether you’re building something that lasts.

According to recent reports, entrepreneurs are idea people. We love trying new things, whether it’s a new campaign or some shiny piece of software that promises to change everything (cough, cough, AI). I’m guilty of it, too. At some point, though, we have to be honest about the difference between what we enjoy doing and what moves the business forward.

Take marketing. You might spend hours making social media content because you enjoy it, while most of your best customers come from referrals. Or you might be convinced a particular service is your bread and butter, only to find out a less exciting offering is generating most of your profit. The numbers don’t always tell the story we want to hear.

So figure out where your best customers are coming from and what they’re buying. A spreadsheet and an honest hour will get you most of the way there. And if you identify something that’s working, do more of it.

This might be my favorite question, because it’s where founders find the quickest wins.

Sources indicate that every business picks up habits over the years: Meetings that made sense two years ago, reports nobody reads, software nobody logs into, services that stay on the menu because they’ve always been there. Individually, none of these seem like a substantial deal. Added up, they eat a surprising amount of time and money, and they eat your attention, which might be the most valuable thing a founder has.

Industry observers note that look at what your team spends time on every week and ask a simple question: If we were starting this business today, would we still do it this way? If the answer is no, why are you doing it now?

Recent findings suggest that I love setting goals. I’m a significant believer in having a vision and building a initiative to get there. I’ve also learned that a new calendar year has never solved an old problem for me. If your sales process is broken in October, a fresh set of goals in January won’t fix it. If you’re spending money on marketing that doesn’t work, a bigger budget just means you’ll waste more of it. And if you’re the bottleneck in every decision, adding more customers is going to make your life harder.

Industry observers note that for the first several years of Bolt, I was in every meeting. That made sense when we were scrappy and fighting for every account. As we grew, I started getting in the way of the systems we’d built to run without me. Now the question I ask my team constantly is, “Do I have to be in this meeting?” Usually the answer is no, and the business runs better because of it.

You don’t have to overhaul the whole firm all at once. Pick one or two things that would make a real difference, like improving your margins, simplifying an offer, documenting a process or finally handing off something you’ve held onto for too long. Then make those changes now, while you still have some time left in the year.

It has been revealed that there’s nothing wrong with pushing hard to finish the year strong. I hope you hit every goal you’ve set. Just don’t get so locked in on a number that you lose sight of what you’re building. Most of us started our businesses to create opportunity and have some control over our time and our future, and a bigger revenue line doesn’t guarantee either one.

Industry observers note that jack was right that you can’t do both at once. So before you lock in next year’s number, ask yourself which season you’re in. If it’s a season to get bigger, run. If it’s a season to get better, give yourself permission to slow down and fix what’s underneath. Either way, choose it on purpose.

A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten. “You can get bigger, or you can get better,” he noted, “but you can’t do both at once.”.

In a recent development, I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid. Work for my marketing agency, Bolt Marketing, slowed overnight, and I was on edge like everyone else. As the dust settled, it became clear that we had enough steady business to keep the lights on, so we made a call. We let go of our most exhausting clients and spent six months working on figuring out who we actually were as a company.

Industry observers note that we tightened up our processes and got honest about our positioning — all the stuff we’d been ignoring. We’ve grown every year since, and I can trace almost all of that growth back to this period of intense focus.

#133307. A ‘mismatch in timing’: Data center power demand is growing 19% a year. The grid is growing 2%

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (987 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Fortune ↗ Open Full Page

A ‘mismatch in timing’: Data center power demand is growing 19% a year. The grid is growing 2%

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (987 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The tech industry is famous for moving fast.
  • Since 2000, power to data centers has risen an average of 19% a year while U.S.
  • According to recent reports, that gap has become one of the biggest bottlenecks facing the AI industry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The tech industry is famous for moving fast. The power grid is famous for not. That collision now sits at the center of the AI buildout, a project estimated to cost trillions: Citigroup projects Significant Tech will spend more than $2.8 trillion on AI infrastructure through 2029, and a Brookings study puts U.S. investment at $10.3 trillion between 2025 and 2032.

The grid isn’t built for that pace. Since 2000, power to data centers has risen an average of 19% a year while U.S. grid capacity has expanded just 2% annually, according to an analysis by insurance broker Howden. Data center power use is growing 10 times faster than the system meant to supply it.

According to recent reports, that gap has become one of the biggest bottlenecks facing the AI industry. And after this month’s midterms, in which voters rejected data center projects almost everywhere they appeared on the ballot, power is now a political problem, too.

Data centers took about 5% of U.S. grid capacity in 2025. Howden estimates that to hold that share through 2030 at current growth rates, they would have to source up to 58% of their power off the grid, roughly 110 gigawatts, a level the firm itself considers unlikely.

According to recent reports, consumption tells the same story. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory projects data centers could use as much as 12% of U.S. electricity by 2028, about six times their 1.9% share in 2018, before the AI boom.

Recent findings suggest that rob Gramlich, president of consulting firm Grid Strategies, told Fortune in September that there’s a real “mismatch in timing” between how quickly data centers want power and how quickly the grid can expand. Grid capacity is slow to build because thousands of interconnected parts must work together, he said, which requires “deliberate study and planning” that can take years.

Sources indicate that the industry is also rusty. After roughly 25 years of little growth in power demand, Gramlich said, utilities “got out of practice on building latest infrastructure.”.

Kathryn Burke, who leads U.S. specialty energy and power growth at insurance firm Marsh, told Fortune she expects around 50% to 60% of data center projects to be delayed beyond the one-to-two-year timelines developers are counting on.

Recent findings suggest that public backlash over grid strain and rising residential electricity prices has added a second hurdle. On Nov. 3, voters rejected data center development in 40 of 41 local ballot measures, the same night Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress.

Opposition runs deepest among the young. A University of Pennsylvania Annenberg Public Policy Center survey conducted this summer found that 70% of adults under 30 oppose new data centers in their area, compared with 61% of all adults.

Voters’ fears aren’t unfounded. Northern Virginia hosts the world’s largest concentration of data centers, and Virginia sells 59% of its electricity to commercial customers, including data center clients. As of 2025, commercial energy demand exceeds residential demand in 23 states and Washington, D.C.

A study in Nature Energy by Cornell University researchers Cheng Feng and Fengqi You found that data centers raised wholesale power prices unevenly. In California’s southern Bay Area, data centers were estimated to lift wholesale prices by nearly 20% in 2025; around Dallas–Fort Worth, the increase approached 17%.

Across the four grids studied, the researchers found that data centers paid only 38% of the infrastructure costs tied to their growth in 2025: $3.12 billion of an $8.25 billion bill.

Wholesale prices make up only about 30% to 50% of a household bill, but experts say residential customers will end up covering part of the AI buildout. The Cornell researchers found the costs land hardest on lower-income and rural households, a pattern they call a “paradoxical mismatch.”.

“The idea of now having to grow up and compete in terms of water prices and energy prices with a tech company is not something I can say I’m excited about,” Elijah Lee, an 18-year-old organizer with the Gen Z advocacy group Voters of Tomorrow, told Fortune before the midterms.

Tech companies are adapting by moving into energy themselves, under a model the industry calls “bring your own power.”.

It has been revealed that some states now require it. In August, Delaware became the first state to legislatively enact a “bring your own generation” policy, requiring large energy users such as data centers to produce or secure 100% of the power they use, including a share of clean energy, within 10 years of starting operations.

In a recent development, president Donald Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge asks signers to “build, bring, or buy” the upcoming-generation resources and electricity they need. Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle and xAI signed in March, and more than 200 utilities, cooperatives, developers and Republican governors have since joined. The pledge is not binding.

On-site generation is still small but growing fast. BloombergNEF counted just 2 gigawatts of on-site gas generation operating at data centers worldwide as of March. It has since tracked 181 gigawatts of announced gas-fired generation proposed alongside data centers, more than 90% of it in the U.S.

Industry observers note that spaceX, for one, has proposed a roughly $24 billion supercomputing facility and gas-fired power plant at Starbase, Texas. The shift carries a climate cost: planned gas plants for data centers could raise U.S. power-sector emissions by 20%, according to a Bloomberg News analysis published by Fortune.

It isn’t a cure-all. Data center development experts say the model isn’t a long-term solution because major swings in power demand at AI data centers can cause outages and damage on-site generation equipment.

The next tests come rapidly. Democrats take control of congressional committees in January. Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa has proposed a moratorium on fresh data center development, and Ohio, which already has 125 local data center moratoriums, is set to add more.

While those buildouts are planned, none are promised.

#133306. The 5 Little Habits That Made a Bigger Difference in My Business Than I Expected

The 5 Little Habits That Made a Bigger Difference in My Business Than I Expected

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1957 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
